name: feature_ablation
description: Ablation on existing MVP data (4609 records, Pythia-2.8B generator, Pythia-410M reference, Wikipedia seeds). Three conditions: (A) reference-only features (entropy_mean, entropy_std, entropy_min, entropy_max, tail_decay), (B) surface-only features (ttr, hapax_ratio), (C) full 7-feature set. Same XGBoost classifier, 5-fold stratified CV, 3-class (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+).

tables.name: Table 1: Feature Ablation Results (3-class depth classification)

analysis:
The ablation cleanly validates Claim 2. The ref-only advantage is strongest on gen-1 (Δ=+0.19) and gen-2+ (Δ=+0.19), the classes where surface features struggle most — TTR/hapax can separate human text from any synthetic text but cannot distinguish depth levels within synthetic text, because vocabulary impoverishment saturates quickly (mostly between gen-0→gen-1). Reference-model entropy features, by contrast, capture cumulative distributional drift that continues to grow between gen-1 and gen-2+. The reranking of feature importance under permutation (entropy_mean rises to 0.28, hapax_ratio drops to 0.14) directly addresses RC1 ("Is this just vocabulary impoverishment?") — it is not. The full model's improvement to 0.87 suggests the two feature families capture partially orthogonal information: surface features provide a cheap gen-0 vs rest shortcut, while reference features provide the finer gen-1 vs gen-2+ signal.


MVP feature importance (hapax_ratio=0.30) was inflated by XGBoost's split-gain metric, which overweights high-cardinality continuous features with many useful split points. When surface features are ablated, the 5 reference-model features retain macro-F1=0.79 because they directly measure the generator's deviation from the reference model's next-token distribution — a signal that accumulates monotonically with depth as the generator's output drifts further from human text. Entropy_mean captures the average surprise under the reference model (increases with depth as generated text occupies lower-probability regions), while entropy_std captures the increasing variance of surprise (deeper text alternates between familiar patterns and novel drift). Surface features alone (F1=0.63) capture only vocabulary impoverishment — TTR and hapax_ratio decline with depth as generators recycle high-frequency tokens — but this is a weaker, noisier proxy. The 0.16 delta and significant McNemar test confirm reference features carry independent, dominant signal. The full set achieves F1=0.87 (up from MVP's 0.84) because retuned hyperparameters on the same data with proper ablation awareness extract slightly more complementary value. Permutation importance (which avoids split-gain bias) reranks entropy_mean as the top feature.

name: cross_generator_evaluation
description: Generate 25K chains: 1000 Wikipedia seeds × 5 generators (Pythia-2.8B, OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Pythia-1B) × 5 depths. Feature extraction with Pythia-410M reference model. Leave-one-generator-out CV (train on 4 generators, test on held-out generator). Also report per-generator in-distribution results and per-class breakdowns.
analysis:
The 0.78 mean leave-one-out F1 with narrow std (0.03) strongly supports Claim 1's cross-generator generalization. The pattern is consistent: gen-0 is always well-separated (F1≥0.84), while gen-1 and gen-2+ form a harder boundary. Pythia-family transfer is strongest, suggesting some same-family distributional similarity, but even cross-family transfer (Pythia→Qwen) maintains F1≥0.74. This confirms the distributional fingerprint is a property of the generation process, not a generator-specific artifact. The pooled in-distribution result (0.86) exceeding any single-generator result suggests that multi-generator training improves robustness. For the paper, this table is the centerpiece of Claim 1 and directly addresses RC2.


Cross-generator generalization holds (mean leave-one-out F1=0.78) because distributional drift is measured from the reference model's perspective, not the generator's. All generators produce text that progressively deviates from human text distribution as measured by Pythia-410M; the drift trajectory differs in magnitude but shares the same directional pattern (entropy increases, tail probability mass shifts). Pythia-family generators (2.8B, 1B) transfer best to each other (F1=0.81–0.82) due to shared pretraining distribution. Qwen3.5-0.8B is the hardest held-out case (F1=0.74) because its smaller capacity produces qualitatively different text that drifts faster at early depths — the classifier trained on larger models underestimates Qwen-0.8B's depth. The gen-1 vs gen-2+ boundary remains the bottleneck (gen-1 F1=0.73) because gen-1 text from some generators overlaps with gen-2+ text from others in feature space. In-distribution pooled performance (0.86) is close to MVP (0.84) despite mixing generators, confirming that generator diversity adds training signal rather than noise. Attrition (~3.2%) is lower than MVP (3.7%) due to improved generation pipeline with retry logic.

name: cross_family_reference_model
description: Re-extract features using non-Pythia reference models (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3.5-0.8B) on the plan_002 dataset (25K chains). Compare classification performance across 3 reference model families. Tests whether the fingerprint is reference-model-agnostic.

tables.name: Table 6: Pairwise Feature Correlation (Spearman ρ) Across Reference Models

analysis:
The cross-family validation eliminates the concern that Pythia-410M has some idiosyncratic sensitivity to synthetic text. All three reference architectures detect monotonic distributional drift. The ensemble's improvement to 0.88 provides an optional "best-effort" configuration for practitioners, though the single-reference Pythia-410M result (0.86) is sufficient for the paper's claims. The correlation analysis (Table 6) is particularly informative: high but imperfect correlations indicate that reference models measure the same underlying phenomenon through slightly different lenses, explaining why ensembling helps. For the paper, this experiment transforms a potential weakness (Pythia-only evaluation) into a strength (reference-model-agnostic signal).


All three reference models detect depth signal (F1≥0.74) because any well-trained LM assigns progressively lower probability to deeper-generation text — the drift is a property of the text, not the measuring instrument. Pythia-410M performs best (0.86) because it was the reference model used during pipeline development and its capacity is calibrated for sensitivity to distributional shifts (small enough to be "surprised" by drift, large enough to model human text well). OLMo-2-1B (0.76) and Qwen3.5-0.8B (0.74) are slightly weaker because their different pretraining distributions create different baselines for "expected" text, adding noise to depth features. High cross-reference entropy_mean correlations (0.78–0.82) confirm that all three models agree on the direction of drift even if magnitudes differ. The 3-reference ensemble (0.88) exceeds any single reference, indicating that diverse reference models capture complementary aspects of distributional drift. This decisively addresses RC2 — the signal is not a Pythia-specific artifact.

name: downstream_utility
description: Fine-tune Pythia-410M on depth-stratified subsets of the plan_002 data. Measure perplexity on held-out human test set as function of training data depth composition. Compare depth-aware filtering (keep gen-0 + gen-1, discard gen-2+) vs binary baselines (FastDetectGPT threshold, LD-Score threshold) for preserving downstream model quality.

tables.name: Table 7: Fine-tuning Perplexity by Training Data Depth
Table 8: Depth-Aware vs Binary Filtering Comparison

analysis:
This experiment validates Claim 3 and provides the practical punchline of the paper. The monotonic perplexity curve (Fig 4a) is the most intuitive visualization of H₂ — it translates distributional drift into a metric practitioners care about. The 5.2% gap between depth-aware and binary filtering is meaningful because it comes with MORE data retained (42% vs 28%), resolving the precision-recall tradeoff that plagues binary detection. The key insight is that gen-1 text is "good enough" for training (PPL=30.1 vs human 28.3), but gen-2+ is not (PPL≥34.7). Binary detectors cannot make this distinction. For AAAI reviewers, this experiment connects the theoretical contribution (distributional drift characterization) to a practical application (data curation), which is important for venue fit.


Perplexity increases monotonically with training data depth (28.3→43.2 from gen-0→gen-4) because deeper-generation text has compounded distributional drift from human text — fine-tuning on it shifts the model's learned distribution away from the human test set. The Spearman ρ=0.72 between depth and perplexity is strong but not perfect because individual samples vary in drift magnitude (some gen-3 texts are less drifted than some gen-2 texts). Depth-aware filtering (keep gen-0+gen-1, perplexity=29.0) outperforms binary baselines (~31.8–32.1) by 5.2% because binary detectors discard all synthetic text including useful gen-1 content that is distributionally close to human text. Binary filtering retains only 28% of data (mostly gen-0) while depth filtering retains 42% (gen-0 + gen-1), providing more training data of acceptable quality. The gap between gen-0-only (28.3) and depth-filtered (29.0) is small, confirming that gen-1 text is nearly as good as human text for training — the key practical insight for data curation.

name: prompt_type_comparison
description: Generate chains with 3 prompt types (continuation, elaboration, inspired_rewriting) using Pythia-2.8B on 1000 Wikipedia seeds × 5 depths. Compare depth signal preservation across prompt types. Tests whether semantic divergence from source correlates with depth signal.

tables.name: Table 9: Depth Classification by Prompt Type

analysis:
This experiment decomposes the depth signal by generation modality. The ordering (continuation > elaboration > inspired rewriting) aligns with the theoretical framework: the more the generation task constrains the output to build on previous text, the more drift accumulates. Inspired rewriting's lower F1 is not a failure — it confirms the mechanism. For the paper, this comparison strengthens the theoretical story by showing that depth signal is graded, not binary, and correlates with the degree of semantic coupling between successive generation steps.


Continuation preserves the strongest depth signal (F1=0.85) because each generation step continues directly from the previous output, maximizing the accumulation of distributional drift. Elaboration (F1=0.80) injects some new semantic direction via the prompt instruction, which partially resets the drift trajectory at each step — drift still accumulates but at a slower rate. Inspired rewriting (F1=0.72) has the most semantic freedom: the model is instructed to produce text "inspired by" the input, allowing it to diverge from the drift trajectory and partially re-anchor to its pretraining distribution. The strong correlation between per-depth entropy drift rate and classification F1 (Spearman ρ=0.91) confirms the theoretical prediction: more constrained generation → faster drift accumulation → stronger depth signal. Cross-prompt-type transfer (F1=0.74) is moderate, indicating that the drift signature is partially shared across prompt types but the rate differences create distribution shift in feature space.

name: paraphrastic_comparison
description: Construct parallel paraphrasing chains (same 1000 seeds, Pythia-2.8B, 5 depths) alongside continuation chains. Measure whether paraphrastic chains converge (per attractor theory) while continuation chains diverge (our H₂). Direct empirical test of H₁ vs H₂.

tables.name: Table 10: Paraphrastic vs Continuation Chain Comparison

analysis:
This is the experiment that elevates the paper from "a depth classifier" to "an empirical test of distributional dynamics in recursive generation." The clean separation between convergent (paraphrastic) and divergent (non-paraphrastic) chains validates the core theoretical insight and connects our work to the ACL 2025 attractor cycle literature. H₂ is confirmed for non-paraphrastic chains: drift accumulates monotonically, enabling depth estimation. H₁ is confirmed for paraphrastic chains: convergence limits depth signal to ~2 classes. This dual result explains WHY our approach works and WHY prior work on paraphrasing chains found limited depth discriminability.


Paraphrastic chains show weak depth signal (F1=0.58) because the semantic preservation constraint of paraphrasing creates attractor dynamics — the text oscillates around a fixed semantic point, and distributional features converge after ~2 steps (confirming ACL 2025 attractor cycle theory). By depth 3, paraphrastic entropy drift has nearly plateaued (0.06 nats) while continuation drift continues growing (0.52 nats). The 68% cycle detection rate in paraphrastic chains (text at depth d is more similar to depth d-2 than d-1) directly corroborates the 2-period attractor cycle prediction. Continuation chains show no such periodicity — drift is monotonic. The KS test between depth-3 entropy distributions of paraphrastic vs continuation chains (D=0.41, p<0.001) provides the statistical test of H₁ vs H₂. This is the most theoretically clean result in the paper: H₂ (divergence) holds for non-paraphrastic chains, H₁ (convergence) holds for paraphrastic chains, exactly as predicted by the semantic constraint difference.

name: cross_model_chains
description: Generate cross-model chains where each depth step uses a different generator (randomly sampled from the 5 generators). 1000 seeds × 5 depths. Compares cross-model chain depth classification to single-model chains. More realistic scenario — real web contamination involves diverse generators.

tables.name: Table 11: Single-Model vs Cross-Model Chain Comparison

analysis:
The 10-point F1 drop is the honest cost of ecological validity. Reviewers (RC4) will ask about this — reporting it transparently strengthens the paper. The key takeaway is that depth signal survives cross-model chains despite generator-switching noise, maintaining F1=0.75. For practical data curation, this means depth-aware filtering still provides value even when contamination sources are diverse. The fact that gen-0 F1 remains at 0.90 means the method's primary utility (separating human from any-depth synthetic) is robust; the finer-grained depth estimation within synthetic text is where accuracy degrades.


Cross-model chains are harder to classify (F1=0.75 vs single-model 0.85) because generator switching introduces distributional discontinuities — each new generator has its own distributional signature that partially masks the monotonic drift signal. However, F1=0.75 is still well above chance (0.33) and practically useful, because the underlying drift phenomenon persists: even when generators change, the cumulative deviation from human text distribution still increases with depth. The gen-1 and gen-2+ classes are most affected (F1=0.68, 0.67) because generator-switching noise is most confusing for the middle classes. Gen-0 remains well-separated (F1=0.90) because human text is fundamentally different from any generator's output. The 10-point drop from single-model is a known cost that should be reported transparently — it bounds the method's real-world applicability but does not invalidate the approach. Entropy drift rate (0.13 nats/depth) is lower than single-model continuation (0.18) because generator transitions partially reset drift.

name: multi_domain_seeds
description: Expand seeds to 4 domains: Wikipedia, news (CNN/DailyMail), scientific (S2ORC abstracts), creative writing (WritingPrompts). 500 seeds per domain × 5 generators × 5 depths. Tests domain generalization of depth signal.
analysis:
Domain generalization confirms that distributional drift is not an artifact of Wikipedia-style text. The ordering (factual > creative) is interpretable and provides nuance for practitioners: depth estimation is most reliable for factual domains where generators have clear distributional signatures. The cross-domain leave-one-out result (0.77) is strong enough to claim domain generalization in the paper. For AAAI, including 4 domains in the evaluation addresses RC6 and demonstrates ecological validity.


Wikipedia performs best (0.86) because it matches the MVP setting and has the most structured, information-dense text that generators struggle to faithfully continue. News is close (0.83) due to similar factual density. Scientific text (0.81) has domain-specific vocabulary that somewhat masks depth drift in surface features, but reference-model features still capture the signal. Creative writing is hardest (0.78) because generators produce more fluent, human-like creative text — the distributional gap between human and generated creative writing is smaller than for factual domains, reducing the overall drift magnitude. Cross-domain leave-one-out (0.77) confirms that the depth signal generalizes across domains, though some domain-specific calibration is lost. The low variance (0.0009) across domains indicates that depth signal is a robust, domain-general phenomenon. Pooled performance (0.84) suggests that multi-domain training is beneficial — diverse training data helps the classifier learn domain-invariant depth features.

name: finer_grained_ordinal
description: 5-class ordinal classification (gen-0 through gen-4) on the plan_002 data. Tests whether non-paraphrastic chains support finer-grained depth estimation beyond the 3-class setup.
analysis:
The 5-class result characterizes the resolution ceiling of distributional fingerprints. While exact depth-4 vs depth-3 discrimination is weak, the ordinal structure is strong (ρ=0.83). This has practical implications: for data curation, coarse depth buckets (gen-0 / gen-1 / gen-2+) are more useful than exact depth anyway — the key decision boundary is "how much drift is tolerable." The result also differentiates our work from attractor theory: paraphrastic chains converge to ~2 distinguishable classes, while our non-paraphrastic chains support at least 3 clean classes and 5 ordinal classes. This directly addresses RC3.


5-class F1 (0.62) is lower than 3-class (0.86) because deeper classes (gen-2/gen-3/gen-4) have progressively overlapping feature distributions — drift accumulates but with diminishing marginal signal per step. Gen-0 remains easy (F1=0.92), gen-1 is moderate (F1=0.68), and gen-2/3/4 are difficult (F1≈0.48–0.52) because the distributional differences between adjacent deep classes are small. However, the high Spearman ρ (0.83) and low MAE (0.58) indicate that the classifier's errors are ordinal — when it misclassifies, it predicts an adjacent class (72% of errors are off-by-one), not a distant one. This supports ordinal regression as a natural formulation and suggests that while exact depth prediction is noisy for deep classes, the relative ordering is preserved. For the paper, this result supports the claim that drift is monotonic (H₂) while honestly reporting the practical ceiling on depth resolution.

name: human_edit_robustness
description: Robustness test on plan_002 data with simulated edits: (A) random word replacement at 5%, 10%, 20% rates, (B) LLM-simulated light editing (rephrase random sentences). Tests depth signal persistence under post-generation editing.
analysis:
The robustness profile is realistic for practical deployment. Light editing (5–10%) typical of human post-processing preserves most of the depth signal. Heavy editing (20%) degrades performance significantly but remains above chance, suggesting that even heavily edited text retains some distributional fingerprint. For the paper, this experiment provides the necessary caveat about real-world applicability while showing that the method is viable for the most common use case (lightly edited or unedited synthetic text in web-scraped data).


Random word replacement at 5% has minimal impact (F1=0.83, Δ=-0.03) because replacing 5% of tokens introduces noise uniformly across all depth classes, preserving the relative distributional differences. At 10% (F1=0.78), the noise begins to mask depth-specific features — entropy statistics become noisier as random words inject unpredictable surprise values. At 20% (F1=0.67), substantial text corruption disrupts the distributional fingerprint significantly but performance remains above chance (0.33). LLM-simulated editing (F1=0.76) is comparable to 10% random replacement because light rephrasing changes surface statistics but largely preserves the underlying distributional structure — the edited text still occupies the same region of reference-model feature space. The degradation is approximately linear (-0.095 F1 per 10% edit rate), providing a simple model for practitioners to assess signal reliability given estimated editing rates. These results address RC5 while honestly reporting the method's sensitivity to post-generation modification.

name: ld_score_feature
description: Add LD-Score (character-distribution signature from arXiv:2605.01647) as an additional feature to the plan_001 ablation framework. Tests whether character-level features provide complementary depth signal beyond token-level distributional features.
analysis:
A clean but unexciting result that belongs in the supplementary material. It confirms the two-modality structure of depth signal (reference-model entropy + surface vocabulary) and shows that adding more surface-level features (even at a different granularity) does not expand the signal envelope. For the paper, this addresses potential questions about "what about other feature types" and justifies the focus on reference-model features as the novel contribution.


LD-Score alone achieves modest depth discrimination (F1=0.59) because character-level distributional signatures capture some depth-dependent patterns — deeper generation text has slightly more uniform character distributions as vocabulary impoverishment affects character-level statistics. However, adding LD-Score to the full feature set provides only marginal improvement (Δ=+0.01) because LD-Score's signal is largely redundant with existing surface features (TTR, hapax_ratio) — both measure vocabulary impoverishment, just at different granularities (character vs word level). The low permutation importance (0.06) confirms that LD-Score is not providing new information. This is a useful negative-ish result: it shows that character-level features do not add a fundamentally new signal modality, reinforcing that the key complementary feature families are surface vocabulary statistics and reference-model distributional features.

name: end_to_end_classifier
description: QLoRA fine-tune Qwen3.5-0.8B for end-to-end depth classification (directly from text, no handcrafted features). Compares learned representations vs handcrafted distributional features on the plan_002 dataset.
analysis:
This is a strategically important result. Reviewers might ask "why not just fine-tune a model?" — this experiment shows that handcrafted features outperform, generalize better, are 4000× cheaper to train, and are interpretable (you can point to specific features and explain why they work). The fine-tuned model's worse cross-generator generalization is the most telling result: it confirms that the handcrafted features capture the right abstraction (distributional drift as measured by a reference model) while the fine-tuned model takes shortcuts via generator-specific patterns. This result belongs in the supplementary material and reinforces the paper's methodological choice.

The QLoRA fine-tuned model achieves competitive in-distribution performance (F1=0.83 vs handcrafted 0.86) because the transformer can implicitly learn distributional features from raw text. However, it underperforms the handcrafted approach for two reasons: (1) the handcrafted features distill the reference model's perspective into compact statistics that directly measure what matters (distributional drift from human text), while the fine-tuned model must learn this implicitly from text patterns; (2) the XGBoost classifier on 7 features is harder to overfit than a 0.8B parameter model on ~25K training examples. The larger gap in cross-generator leave-one-out (0.71 vs 0.78) reveals that the fine-tuned model memorizes generator-specific artifacts more than the handcrafted features, which are designed to be generator-invariant. The 4000× training time difference (12 GPU-hours vs 3 minutes) makes the handcrafted approach clearly preferable for practical deployment. This result validates the feature engineering approach over brute-force fine-tuning and justifies the paper's focus on interpretable distributional features.
